1→# Local use-case runner

Date: 2026-08-31
Status: ready-for-agent
Source: [wayfinder map](map.md)

## Post-spec change (2026-08-31)

The grill skill lives in **doraval** (`skills/`).
10→It does not live in the kit.
`dora harness new` starts it.

## Tickets

- [#79](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/79) Harness group on the closed tree
- [#80](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/80) Routine folder + list + open (blocked by #79)
- [#81](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/81) Grill skill + `dora harness new` (blocked by #80)
- [#82](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/82) Boot, pause, resume (blocked by #80)
- [#83](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/83) Docs lockstep (blocked by #81 and #82)
20→
Frontier: #79. Next session: `/implement` #79. Clear context between tickets.

## Problem Statement

An internal Scalekit teammate wants a use case to keep running after the chat closes.

They already have LLM credits. They can paste a Scalekit Agent Gateway MCP URL. They do not want a new CLI. They do not want a shared team bot. They do not want Slack, Discord, or Webflow baked into the runner.

Today they can grill a use case in a chat. Then the chat ends. Nothing runs on an interval. Tokens and tools are not wired for a night pass. There is no saved object they can pause or boot again.
30→
## Solution

The teammate opens **Dora**. Dora is the front desk.

A **grill skill** (authored in this kit) turns a use case into a **routine**. A routine is a saved folder at `~/.dora/harness/<slug>/`. It is the only product object.

Dora then helps run that prompt **once**. After that one pass, `dora harness boot` starts **Hermes** only: the Hermes gateway as a machine service, plus one Hermes cron job. Dora exits. Hermes runs a **loop**: the same prompt, on an interval.

Tools go through **Scalekit Agent Gateway MCP**. Slack, Discord, and Webflow are connectors on a use case. They are not part of the harness.
40→
The teammate brings their own LLM credits. This spec describes the product. It does not install it.

## User Stories

1. As an internal Scalekit teammate, I want to open Dora rather than Hermes, so that I have one front desk for create, boot, pause, and list.
2. As a teammate, I want use-case verbs under `dora harness`, so that I do not mix them with `dora review`.
3. As a teammate, I want `dora harness new` to start the grill skill, so that I do not write a routine by hand.
4. As a teammate, I want the grill to ask what the use case does, so that the unattended prompt is specific.
5. As a teammate, I want the grill to collect skills to **run**, skills to **refer to**, and the Scalekit Agent Gateway URL, so that a night pass has what it needs.
50→6. As a teammate, I want a default shared MCP URL that I paste once, so that I do not paste it for every routine.
7. As a teammate, I want a routine to override that URL, so that one odd job can use a different gateway.
8. As a teammate, I want the grill to pick a slug I can read, so that I can type `dora harness boot ooo-calendar`.
9. As a teammate, I want to rename the slug, so that a bad first name is not permanent.
10. As an agent running the grill, I want to mirror `grill-with-docs` (interview plus a paper trail), so that answers are not lost in chat.
11. As an agent running the grill, I want `writing-for-agents` to write the full unattended prompt after the interview, so that the night text is written for an agent, not a human chat.
12. As a teammate, I want one live test pass before anything is scheduled, so that a bad prompt does not run every hour.
13. As a teammate, I want Dora to print the one-pass command, so that I can run it myself.
14. As a teammate, I want Dora to offer an interactive flow for that one pass, so that I do not have to copy a command if I do not want to.
15. As a teammate without Hermes, I want Dora to print official Hermes install steps plus the command, so that I know what to install. I do not want Dora to install Hermes.
60→16. As a teammate without Hermes, I want Dora to refuse to fake a test run, so that I am not told it worked when it did not.
17. As a teammate, I want Dora to write the routine folder only after the one pass is done (or I accept the printed command path), so that disk does not hold a scheduled job I never saw.
18. As a teammate, I want a routine to live at `~/.dora/harness/<slug>/`, so that I know where it is.
19. As a teammate, I want the routine to hold the prompt, skill directories, MCP URL, interval, and max tick, so that boot has one source.
20. As a teammate, I want the default interval to be every 1 hour, so that I do not set a schedule for a first job.
21. As a teammate, I want the default max tick to be 10 minutes, so that one stuck pass cannot run forever.
22. As a teammate, I want both fields to be configurable per routine, so that a tight job can run more often.
23. As a teammate, I want `dora harness boot <slug>` to start that routine, so that I do not touch Hermes cron by hand.
24. As a teammate, I want bare `dora harness boot` to list existing routines and let me pick one or create, so that I do not have to remember slugs.
25. As a teammate, I want boot to start the Hermes gateway as a machine service, so that the loop keeps ticking after Dora exits.
70→26. As a teammate, I want boot to write one Hermes cron job from the routine, so that Hermes owns the timer.
27. As a teammate, I want Dora to exit after boot, so that I can close that terminal.
28. As a teammate, I want another terminal to work for pause and list, so that I do not attach to the first session.
29. As a teammate, I want `dora harness pause <slug>` to pause that cron job only, so that other routines on the same gateway keep running.
30. As a teammate, I want pause to leave the gateway up, so that I do not kill every loop to stop one.
31. As a teammate, I want a pause to mean “skip later ticks,” so that a pass that already started may finish.
32. As a teammate, I want `dora harness resume <slug>` to start later ticks again, so that pause is reversible.
33. As a teammate, I want closing the laptop to be sleep, not pause, so that I do not think I paused when the clock just stopped.
34. As a teammate, I want to know that cron does not run while the host sleeps, so that I do not expect night work from a closed Mac.
35. As a teammate, I want due jobs to be able to fire on wake if they are not paused, so that I understand what happens after I open the lid.
80→36. As a teammate, I want `dora harness list` to show routines and whether each job is running or paused, so that I can see state.
37. As a teammate, I want `dora harness open <slug>` to open that routine folder, so that I can read or edit the prompt.
38. As a teammate, I want the first MCP connect to be Hermes OAuth / magic link, so that Scalekit can store provider tokens.
39. As a teammate, I want Dora to stay off that magic link, so that Dora does not sit in the OAuth path.
40. As a teammate, I want night runs to reuse `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/` after one login, so that I am not at the keyboard every hour.
41. As a teammate, I want a refresh failure to stop and ask me to run `hermes mcp login`, so that a dead token does not look like a silent success.
42. As a teammate, I want a dead Scalekit connected account to stop and ask me to open the link again, so that I can fix the provider side.
43. As a teammate, I want the cron job toolset to include `mcp-<server>`, so that Scalekit tools are actually on the night pass.
44. As a teammate, I want Slack, Discord, and Webflow to be optional connectors on a use case, so that the harness does not assume Slack.
45. As a teammate, I want a loop to mean “same prompt on an interval,” so that I do not confuse it with polling one chat app.
90→46. As a teammate, I want to bring my own LLM credits, so that the runner does not sell inference.
47. As a teammate, I want skill directories to be pluggable, so that I can point at the skills this job needs.
48. As a teammate, I do not want skillkit to be the default, so that a laptop without skillkit still works.
49. As a teammate, I want an optional later copy of a routine into skillkit, so that sharing is possible without being required.
50. As a teammate, I want an optional later way to point Dora at a repo of routines, so that a team folder can land later.
51. As a teammate, I want optional `dora review` on attached skill directories, so that I can check those skills if I want. The product must work if I skip that review.
52. As a teammate, I want secrets kept off git, so that an optional remote does not leak tokens.
53. As a teammate, I want an optional git remote on the routine folder later, so that I can share the prompt and not the secrets.
54. As a teammate, I want Hermes to be the only runtime in this spec, so that I do not get a Claude / Grok / OpenCode runner in v1.
55. As a teammate, I want missing Hermes to print install steps and stop on boot too, so that boot does not fail in a cryptic way.
100→56. As a doraval maintainer, I want the grill skill in `skills/` and shipped only after `dora review --quick` exits 0, so that a draft does not land in the catalog.
57. As a doraval maintainer, I want the grill skill to follow writing-for-agents (imperative, no “You are,” no em-dashes), so that the night text is written for an agent.
58. As a doraval maintainer, I want the shipped Doraval skill catalog to name `dora harness` when the group ships, so that the Runner map does not lie.
59. As a doraval maintainer, I want `harness` added as a core command group (`defineGroup`), so that the verbs are real CLI, not a plugin.
60. As a doraval maintainer, I want root verbs like `dora review` unchanged, so that existing Dora users are not moved.
61. As a first reader, I want the spec, docs, and grill wording to talk to an internal teammate, so that I am not sold a customer product yet.
62. As a later reader, I want a path that is not locked to Scalekit customers only (anyone with Dora, Hermes, and an MCP URL), so that opening up later does not require a rewrite of the objects. This spec does not write that later wording.
63. As a teammate, I want one machine and one user, so that I do not need a company fleet setup.
64. As a teammate, I want no first sample use case forced by this spec, so that the harness stays generic.

110→## Implementation Decisions

- One repo plus one runtime. Doraval authors the grill skill under `skills/` and grows the `dora harness` group. Hermes is configured, not forked. The kit does not own this work.
- The user-facing object is a **routine**. Hermes still stores a cron **job**. The teammate hears “routine.”
- Routine path: `~/.dora/harness/<slug>/`. Slug comes from the grill and may be renamed. Commands take the slug.
- Routine contents (contract, not file names): unattended prompt, skill directories to run, skill directories to refer to, MCP URL, interval, max tick. The shape is extensible. Secrets do not live in a file that an optional git remote would publish.
- Default schedule: every 1 hour. Default max tick: 10 minutes (Hermes 600s). Both are per-routine and may be changed later by the grill or by `dora harness`.
- `dora harness` verbs: `new`, `boot`, `pause`, `resume`, `list`, `open`. `resume` is required because pause must reverse. `open` opens the routine folder.
- Bare `boot` lists routines and lets the teammate pick one or start create (same path as `new`). `boot <slug>` boots that routine.
- Boot sequence: if Hermes is missing, print official install steps and stop. If Hermes is present, ensure the gateway is running as a machine service, write one cron job from the routine (toolset includes `mcp-<server>`), then exit. Dora does not own a timer.
120→- Pause calls `hermes cron pause` for that job. Job state becomes `paused`. Gateway stays up. A running pass may finish. Resume calls `hermes cron resume`.
- Laptop close is host sleep. Official Hermes: cron does not run while the host sleeps. Sleep is not pause.
- Scalekit is a normal HTTP MCP server in Hermes (`url` plus `auth: oauth`). It is not the Nous Tool Gateway. The teammate pastes the MCP URL. Dora does not mint Virtual MCP session tokens with API keys.
- First connect is Hermes OAuth / magic link. Scalekit stores provider tokens. Hermes stores MCP login under `~/.hermes/mcp-tokens/`. Later ticks reuse those files. Refresh is automatic while the refresh token is valid.
- Refresh fail or missing cache: stop and tell the human to run `hermes mcp login <server>`. A dead connected account: stop and tell the human to open the provider link again. Cron has no TTY. Do not pretend a browser flow will work at night.
- Grill skill: we author it in doraval under `skills/`. Ship with `dora review --quick` on that skill directory. Do not draft it in the kit. Do not update kit `ask-saif`.
- Grill shape: mirror `grill-with-docs`. Pragmatic gate before save: skills to run, skills to refer to, Scalekit Agent Gateway URL. Then `writing-for-agents` writes the unattended prompt. Then one test pass (print the command, or an interactive flow). Then write the routine folder.
- Later, steal Warp skill-doctor checks that fit. Those checks are not a v1 gate.
- Dora may later copy a routine to skillkit, or point at a repo of routines. Not required for v1.
- Optional `dora review` on attached skill directories. Skip is fine.
130→- User brings LLM credits. This spec does not provision a model key.
- Do not write loop product terms into kit `CONTEXT.md`. Kit glossary stays the language of the kit.
- First wording is for an internal teammate. Do not pick a first sample use case.

## Testing Decisions

A good test checks what a teammate can see or what Dora writes. It does not check Hermes internals. It does not start a live gateway in CI. It does not run a real Scalekit OAuth dance.

### Seams

140→1. **Primary seam: `dora harness` CLI (doraval).** Assert help text, missing-Hermes install steps, routine folder write, and the Hermes commands Dora would run for boot, pause, resume, and list. Prefer doraval’s existing command-tree / CLI tests.
2. **Secondary seam: grill skill in doraval `skills/`.** Assert `dora review <skill-dir> --quick` exits 0. Also assert the skill names the pragmatic gate and the one-pass-then-save order. Do not automate the interview.
3. **Shared artifact: routine folder contract.** The folder is the seam between Dora and Hermes. Assert slug, prompt, skill dirs, MCP URL, interval, and max tick are present. Do not assert Hermes job JSON schema beyond what Dora is specified to write.

### Modules under test

- Doraval `harness` group (behavior at the CLI).
- Grill skill (review plus the documented gate and order).
- Routine folder writer (contract above).

150→### Prior art

- Doraval: `dora review --quick` on the grill skill. Closed command tree plus CLI tests for each verb. New group follows that pattern.
- No Hermes test double that reimplements cron.

## Out of Scope

- A new CLI beside Dora.
- Hermes Tool Gateway as the Slack (or any connector) path.
- Minting Scalekit session tokens with API keys (Virtual MCP mint path).
160→- Claude, Grok, or OpenCode as the runtime in this spec.
- The whole product as “a kit skill.” The grill skill lives in doraval. The runner is still Dora plus Hermes.
- Picking a first sample use case (Discord, GitHub, or OOO). The spec stays generic.
- Wording and docs for “anyone with the stack.” First reader is an internal teammate.
- Company setup on more than one machine.
- Dora installing Hermes.
- Dora sitting on the magic link / OAuth path.
- Push, webhooks, or a Hermes Slack bot. The interval is the trigger.
- Making skillkit the default skill directory.
- Writing loop terms into kit `CONTEXT.md`. Doraval `CONTEXT.md` may gain routine / harness / loop terms when the group ships.
170→- Shipping the grill skill in this spec session. Spec first. Tickets next.

## Further Notes

Map: [Local use cases](map.md).

Research:

- Loop runners survey: `docs/research/2026-08-28-always-on-loop-runners.md`
- Hermes cron and MCP OAuth: `docs/research/2026-08-29-hermes-cron-mcp-oauth.md`
180→- Dora command growth: `docs/research/2026-08-29-dora-command-extension.md`

Next skill after this spec is accepted: `/to-tickets`. Then `/implement` per ticket in a fresh session.

Hermes is not installed on the author’s machine yet. A live one-pass test waits until a human installs it. That install is a later `/wizard` or a human step. It is not this spec.

subprocess/plugins/OAuth. dora's API path already is that.

FileContent.content:
1→## What it does

`domain-modeling` builds and sharpens a project's **ubiquitous language** while you are designing — challenging a term that conflicts with the glossary, forcing a precise word where you used a vague one, and stress-testing a relationship with a concrete scenario until the boundaries are exact.

It is the **active** discipline, not the passive one. Reading `CONTEXT.md` to borrow its vocabulary is a one-line habit any skill can do; this skill is for when you are *changing* the model. That is what makes it interrupt. It writes a resolved term into `CONTEXT.md` at the moment it is resolved, in the middle of the conversation, rather than producing a tidy glossary at the end — because the batched version is a summary of a [session](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/session), and the inline version is the session's actual output.

## When to reach for it

Type `/domain-modeling`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task fits. In practice, automatic invocation is the weakest part of the skill: when `grill-with-docs` or `wayfinder` say to load it, [models](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/model) frequently load `grilling` and skip this one. If a [grilling](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/grilling) session runs and `CONTEXT.md` is untouched at the end, that is what happened — invoke it by name alongside the other skill.
10→
Reach for it when the *words* are the problem:

| The situation | The move |
| --- | --- |
| Two people mean different things by "cancellation" | `domain-modeling` — pick the canonical term, list the other under `_Avoid_` |
| "Account" is doing three jobs in three files | `domain-modeling` — split it into Customer and User |
| You just made a hard-to-reverse architectural choice | `domain-modeling` — it offers an ADR, if the choice clears the bar |
| The module's *shape* is the problem — where the seam goes, how deep the interface is | [codebase-design](https://aihero.dev/skills-codebase-design) |
| You want the whole plan interrogated before you build | [grill-with-docs](https://aihero.dev/skills-grill-with-docs), which drives this skill underneath |
20→| You want a term looked up, not changed | Nothing. Read `CONTEXT.md`. It is a file. |

## Prerequisites

None up front. The skill writes into two places and creates both lazily:

- **`CONTEXT.md`** at the repo root, created by the first resolved term. In a repo with a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the root, terms go into the per-context `CONTEXT.md` the map points at instead.
- **`docs/adr/`**, created by the first ADR that clears the bar.

Nothing needs to exist before you start, and nothing is created speculatively.
30→
## Two artifacts, two bars

The glossary and the ADR are held to different standards, and conflating them is where most of the trouble in this skill comes from.

| | `CONTEXT.md` | `docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Holds | Terms. What a thing **is**, in one or two sentences, with rejected synonyms under `_Avoid_` | One decision, in one to three sentences: context, choice, reason |
| Bar to write | A vague term became canonical | **All three**: hard to reverse, surprising without context, the result of a real trade-off |
| Written | Inline, the moment the term is settled | Offered, not assumed |
40→| Never holds | Implementation details, a [spec](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/spec), a scratch pad, general programming concepts | A diary of every choice made this session |

Miss any one of the ADR's three tests and there is no ADR. An easily-reversed decision will just get reversed; an unsurprising one is nobody's question; one with no real alternative records that you did the obvious thing.

The `CONTEXT.md` rule is the one to actually hold onto, because it is the one that breaks in the field. **It is a glossary and nothing else.** Left unchecked, models treat "write to `CONTEXT.md`" as permission to persist every answer you give, and the file turns into a running spec — this is the most-reported problem with the skill, across several models.

## Cross-referencing, and where it stops

The move that makes the skill click: when you state how something works, it checks the code and surfaces the contradiction. *"Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"* The language and the code are made to agree, out loud, before either is changed.

50→The limit is worth knowing. It cross-references **code** and the committed `CONTEXT.md`/ADRs, and nothing else. It does not search your issue tracker, so a naming collision that was argued out and deliberately settled in a closed issue months ago gets surfaced as if it were new. There is [an open request](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/717) to fix this; until then, the workaround is to put the instruction in your own `docs/agents/domain.md`, which the skills already read.

## Common questions

**My `CONTEXT.md` is 500 lines. 1,000. 3,000. What do I do?**
The size is a symptom, not the disease — the file has absorbed implementation detail and decisions that were never glossary material. The fix is a direct instruction: `/grill-with-docs make my CONTEXT.md more concise and remove any implementation details from it`. Run it against a bloated file and most of it goes. Only reach for a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` split once the file is genuinely lean and still covers two domains that a reader would not want to hold at once; splitting a bloated file just gives you several bloated files. The skill's guidance here is not yet strong enough to prevent the growth in the first place, and the issue tracking that is still open.

**Why is it `CONTEXT.md` and not `GLOSSARY.md`?**
This is the most-argued naming question in the whole skill set and it has no settled answer. The case against the current name is good: if it is "a glossary and nothing else", `GLOSSARY.md` says so, and — as one reader put it — "with ai agents everything is [context](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/context)". The case for it is the map: `CONTEXT-MAP.md` pointing at several `CONTEXT.md` files reads naturally in a way `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` does not, and `context` is the standing DDD word for a bounded area of the model. At least one person maintains a local fork purely to rename the file. You can do the same, but every other skill in the set looks for `CONTEXT.md`, so a rename means patching all of them.

60→**Where did `/ubiquitous-language` go?**
It was removed, and it was not deprecated. Its job moved into `domain-modeling`, which maintains the whole model continuously rather than dumping a glossary out of one conversation. Vocabulary enforcement got more load-bearing, not less — it now runs underneath grilling, triage and mapping rather than as a separate pass you remember to do.

**How do I get a glossary for a codebase that has none?**
Ask for it explicitly rather than waiting for it to accumulate. `/grill-with-docs help me scaffold my existing repo with a CONTEXT.md` is the documented route; expect a long interrogation — one user reported 50+ questions before the file was in shape. Incidental use builds the glossary far too slowly on a brownfield repo.

**Can I keep the domain model and use my own ADR format?**
Not cleanly today. The glossary half and the ADR half ship in one skill, so a team with an established ADR convention — different template, different location, different naming — gets instructions that conflict with its house style. The current options are to copy the skill locally and edit it, or to override the ADR conventions in your repo's own agent docs. Splitting the two apart is [an open request](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/557).

**Does a glossary actually earn its keep? It is one more artifact to review, and it can go stale.**
70→Sometimes it does not, and it is worth being honest about where. DDD gets less useful the closer it gets to the implementation — the payoff is upstream, in naming and concept alignment, not in aggregates and layer ceremony. Synonym control matters at naming boundaries: module names, table names, status enums, issue titles, CLI commands. It matters much less in ordinary prose. There is also a live objection that domain terms compress communication *between humans* who already share them, and that an agent responds the same way to the plain-English description — on that reading, the glossary's value is keeping you and your reviewers aligned with what the agent is doing, not making the agent better. On a one-day build, skip it. And an unreviewed, agent-authored glossary is worse than none: it becomes confident-sounding lore that later sessions treat as truth.

**Can it turn my vague prompts into domain language for me?**
No, and there is no plan for a skill that does. A domain language you do not understand yourself becomes meaningless drivel once written down. This skill enforces precision once you have the understanding — it does not manufacture vocabulary you do not have. The related trap is using domain words without doing the modelling: right nouns over the wrong conceptual structure produce output that reads correct and is not.

## It's working if

- It stops you mid-sentence to ask which of two things you meant, instead of picking one and moving on.
- `CONTEXT.md` changes **during** the conversation, not in a burst at the end.
- It refuses to write an ADR for something you could undo tomorrow — and says which of the three tests failed.
80→- New entries define what a thing *is* in one or two sentences and name the words you are giving up under `_Avoid_`.

## What it does

`domain-modeling` builds and sharpens a project's **ubiquitous language** while you are designing — challenging a term that conflicts with the glossary, forcing a precise word where you used a vague one, and stress-testing a relationship with a concrete scenario until the boundaries are exact.

It is the **active** discipline, not the passive one. Reading `CONTEXT.md` to borrow its vocabulary is a one-line habit any skill can do; this skill is for when you are *changing* the model. That is what makes it interrupt. It writes a resolved term into `CONTEXT.md` at the moment it is resolved, in the middle of the conversation, rather than producing a tidy glossary at the end — because the batched version is a summary of a [session](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/session), and the inline version is the session's actual output.

## When to reach for it

Type `/domain-modeling`, or the agent reaches for it automatically when a task fits. In practice, automatic invocation is the weakest part of the skill: when `grill-with-docs` or `wayfinder` say to load it, [models](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/model) frequently load `grilling` and skip this one. If a [grilling](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/grilling) session runs and `CONTEXT.md` is untouched at the end, that is what happened — invoke it by name alongside the other skill.

Reach for it when the *words* are the problem:

| The situation | The move |
| --- | --- |
| Two people mean different things by "cancellation" | `domain-modeling` — pick the canonical term, list the other under `_Avoid_` |
| "Account" is doing three jobs in three files | `domain-modeling` — split it into Customer and User |
| You just made a hard-to-reverse architectural choice | `domain-modeling` — it offers an ADR, if the choice clears the bar |
| The module's *shape* is the problem — where the seam goes, how deep the interface is | [codebase-design](https://aihero.dev/skills-codebase-design) |
| You want the whole plan interrogated before you build | [grill-with-docs](https://aihero.dev/skills-grill-with-docs), which drives this skill underneath |
| You want a term looked up, not changed | Nothing. Read `CONTEXT.md`. It is a file. |

## Prerequisites

None up front. The skill writes into two places and creates both lazily:

- **`CONTEXT.md`** at the repo root, created by the first resolved term. In a repo with a `CONTEXT-MAP.md` at the root, terms go into the per-context `CONTEXT.md` the map points at instead.
- **`docs/adr/`**, created by the first ADR that clears the bar.

Nothing needs to exist before you start, and nothing is created speculatively.

## Two artifacts, two bars

The glossary and the ADR are held to different standards, and conflating them is where most of the trouble in this skill comes from.

| | `CONTEXT.md` | `docs/adr/NNNN-slug.md` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Holds | Terms. What a thing **is**, in one or two sentences, with rejected synonyms under `_Avoid_` | One decision, in one to three sentences: context, choice, reason |
| Bar to write | A vague term became canonical | **All three**: hard to reverse, surprising without context, the result of a real trade-off |
| Written | Inline, the moment the term is settled | Offered, not assumed |
| Never holds | Implementation details, a [spec](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/spec), a scratch pad, general programming concepts | A diary of every choice made this session |

Miss any one of the ADR's three tests and there is no ADR. An easily-reversed decision will just get reversed; an unsurprising one is nobody's question; one with no real alternative records that you did the obvious thing.

The `CONTEXT.md` rule is the one to actually hold onto, because it is the one that breaks in the field. **It is a glossary and nothing else.** Left unchecked, models treat "write to `CONTEXT.md`" as permission to persist every answer you give, and the file turns into a running spec — this is the most-reported problem with the skill, across several models.

## Cross-referencing, and where it stops

The move that makes the skill click: when you state how something works, it checks the code and surfaces the contradiction. *"Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible — which is right?"* The language and the code are made to agree, out loud, before either is changed.

The limit is worth knowing. It cross-references **code** and the committed `CONTEXT.md`/ADRs, and nothing else. It does not search your issue tracker, so a naming collision that was argued out and deliberately settled in a closed issue months ago gets surfaced as if it were new. There is [an open request](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/717) to fix this; until then, the workaround is to put the instruction in your own `docs/agents/domain.md`, which the skills already read.

1→# ask-dora skill family

Date: 2026-08-31
Status: ready-for-agent
Source: grill in this repo, 2026-08-31. Glossary: `CONTEXT.md` (ask-dora section).
Issue: [#84](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/84)
Tickets: #85 → then #86 and #87 in parallel → #88 → #89
Related: [Local use-case runner](../local-use-cases/spec.md) and issues #79–#83. This spec does not redo the harness CLI.

10→## Problem Statement

An internal Scalekit teammate opens a coding agent and wants help with Dora.

Today the shipped skill talks only to the Runner. It says: run `dora review --quick`, then fix, until exit 0. That is one job.

The teammate’s real start is a sentence: they type a command and describe an agent they want to run on this machine. Or they ask a normal Dora question (review, fix, unused). There is no one skill that routes both.

The harness already has a grill skill (`grill-routine`) and a routine folder. That grill is not the front door. It does not ask “is this loop-able?” first. It does not check Scalekit connectors. It does not copy skills into the routine. It is not written as a small family.

20→Matt-style idea-to-ship maps do not fit. This product is not “any software idea → ship code.” It is a **routine idea** → a **local** agent that can **loop**.

## Solution

Ship four skills under one add: `npx skills add saif-shines/doraval`.

1. **`ask-dora`** — the only name the human must remember. User-typed router. They type `/ask-dora` plus any Dora question or a routine idea.
2. **`review-with-dora`** — the old Runner loop (review → fix → exit 0). Replaces the skill named `doraval`.
3. **`grilling-for-routine`** — interview for a routine idea. Replaces `grill-routine`.
4. **`writing-for-routine`** — how to write the unattended night prompt. Original text. Same craft as a good agent document (steps, done-when, no second-person). Do not cite or copy another pack.
30→
`discover-connectors` already exists in Scalekit. Point at it. Do not author a second skill with that name.

**Route**

- A Dora job (review, fix, unused, scan) → `review-with-dora` or the matching `dora` verb.
- A **routine idea** (loop, recurring, or an agent that should keep running locally) → the routine flow.

**Routine flow**

40→1. Is it **loop-able**? Can the same prompt run on an interval? If no: say why. Stop. Do not write a routine. Route if it is a normal Dora job.
2. `grilling-for-routine`.
3. Practicality check: live Scalekit connector catalog via `discover-connectors`. Say what exists. Say what an interval job cannot do.
4. `writing-for-routine` writes the night prompt.
5. **Routine copy**: duplicate skill folders into the routine. Source is a name on this machine, a local path, or a GitHub URL. Never edit the original.
6. One live run (print the command, or run it). Missing Hermes: print official install steps. Do not fake a pass.
7. If that run works → **loop** on Hermes. Default interval 1 hour. Dora stays off OAuth. Token fail → `hermes mcp login`.

`dora harness new` starts `ask-dora`, which loads `grilling-for-routine` when the ask is a routine idea.

50→## User Stories

1. As an internal teammate, I want to type `/ask-dora` plus any Dora question, so that I do not have to remember four skill names.
2. As a teammate, I want `/ask-dora` to work when I am not talking about a routine, so that I can still review, fix, or scan.
3. As a teammate, I want `/ask-dora always poll the ooo-holidays channel and create Google Calendar events` to start the routine flow, so that a routine idea has one start.
4. As a teammate, I want the first check to be “is this loop-able?”, so that a webhook or a one-off chat job is not saved as a routine.
5. As a teammate, I want a clear why when an idea is not loop-able, so that I know what to change or which Dora job to run instead.
6. As a teammate, I want no routine folder when the idea is not loop-able, so that disk does not hold a job that cannot loop.
7. As a teammate, I want the grill to ask until the night prompt is specific, so that an unattended pass has enough information.
8. As a teammate, I want the grill to collect skills to run, skills to refer to, and the Scalekit Agent Gateway MCP URL, so that the night pass has a gate.
60→9. As a teammate, I want a default shared MCP URL reused unless I override it, so that I do not paste it every time.
10. As a teammate, I want the agent to look up Scalekit connectors, so that I hear what is possible before the night prompt is written.
11. As a teammate, I want to hear when a needed connector is missing, so that I do not schedule a job that cannot call the tool.
12. As a teammate, I want to hear when an interval job cannot do the idea (push, webhook, human in the loop every tick), so that I do not confuse a loop with a chat app.
13. As a teammate, I want the night prompt written for an agent, so that the loop does not read like a human chat.
14. As a teammate, I want that prompt to use steps and a done-when, so that the night agent can tell finished from not finished.
15. As a teammate, I want no second-person identity in the night prompt, so that the unattended agent is not told “you are.”
16. As a teammate, I want to name a skill, or give a local path, or give a GitHub URL, so that I can bring skills I already have.
17. As a teammate, I want Dora to look up a named skill on this machine first (project `skills/`, then home), so that a short name is enough when the skill is already here.
18. As a teammate, I want Dora to ask for a path or a GitHub URL when the name is missing, so that it does not invent a registry.
70→19. As a teammate, I want those skills copied into the routine, so that later edits do not change the original.
20. As a teammate, I want routine-level edits on the copy only, so that I can tune one job without breaking other jobs.
21. As a teammate, I want one live run before Hermes, so that a bad prompt does not fire every hour.
22. As a teammate, I want the one-pass command printed, so that I can run it in another terminal.
23. As a teammate, I want an offer to run that pass if Hermes is present, so that I do not have to copy the command.
24. As a teammate without Hermes, I want official install steps and no fake pass, so that I am not told it worked.
25. As a teammate, I want the loop to start only after that run works, so that Hermes does not get a failing job.
26. As a teammate, I want the default interval to stay 1 hour, so that I am not forced to pick a schedule first.
27. As a teammate, I want to set the interval after the good run, so that I configure the loop at the moment it becomes real.
28. As a teammate, I want `dora harness boot / pause / resume / list / open` after a routine exists, so that the life of the job has verbs.
80→29. As a teammate, I want Dora off the OAuth / magic-link path, so that a night tick does not wait on a browser.

70→Wrong (the live crash):

```bash
hermes cron create "every 1h" "…" --toolsets mcp-scalekit --timeout 600
hermes --oneshot --toolsets mcp-scalekit "…"   # --oneshot eats --toolsets
```

Official CLI page (newer than 0.20.6) prefers:

```bash
80→hermes chat --oneshot -q "…"
hermes chat --query-file prompt.md --oneshot
```

`chat --query-file` is safer for long unattended prompts (quotes, `$(…)`, backticks arrive verbatim). Dora currently puts the whole prompt on argv.

`hermes chat` also has `--run-budget SECONDS` (wall-clock wrap-up). That is the closest one-pass match for routine `maxTick`. Top-level `-z` on 0.20.6 has **no** `--timeout` and **no** `--run-budget`.

### Cron create (the night job)

90→Local `hermes cron create --help` accepts:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `schedule` (positional) | `30m`, `every 2h`, `0 9 * * *` |
| `prompt` (positional, optional) | Task text |
| `--name` | Human name. Dora uses the slug. Pause/resume/list key off this. |
| `--skill` (repeatable) | Attach a skill |
| `--workdir` | Absolute cwd. Loads `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md` / `.cursorrules`. Omit = no project files. |
| `--model` / `--provider` | User-owned pin. The agent `cronjob` tool cannot set this. |
100→| `--reasoning-effort` | `none` … `ultra` |
| `--deliver` | `origin`, `local`, telegram, discord, … Spec says do not bake Slack/Discord into the harness. |
| `--script` / `--no-agent` | Script-only job. Not our path. |
| `--monitor-script` / `--monitor-url` | Cheap hash gate before the LLM. |
| `--continuity` | Inject previous run output into the next prompt. |
| `--repeat` | Finite count |

**Not on the parser:** `--toolsets`, `--timeout`, `-t`, `--oneshot`. [Issue #24134](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/24134) asked for `--toolsets` on create (v0.13.0). Still open. PR #24145 referenced, not the supported surface.

Schedule without `every` or `*`: Hermes treats a bare `30m` / `1d` as a **one-shot**, then the job goes `[completed]`. Dora wraps with `hermesSchedule()` → `every 1h`. Keep that.
110→
---

## Cron toolsets (how Scalekit actually reaches the night job)

Cron does **not** inherit CLI `--toolsets`.

Resolution order (official cron page + GitHub #23997 / commit `74a5905`):

1. Per-job `enabled_toolsets` on the `cronjob` **tool** (not the CLI).

## Timeouts (spec max tick)

Two different clocks. Do not mix them.

| Knob | What it limits | Default | Dora today |
|------|----------------|---------|------------|
| `HERMES_CRON_TIMEOUT` | **Idle** time with no tool call / token stream. `0` = unlimited. Job may run for hours if it keeps working. | 600s | Not set. `hermesTimeoutSec("10m")` equals 600 but is unused. |
| `cron.script_timeout_seconds` / `HERMES_CRON_SCRIPT_TIMEOUT` | Pre-run **script** only | 3600s | N/A (we are not `--script`) |
| `hermes chat --run-budget SECONDS` | Wall-clock for a conversation run. 80% wrap-up notice. | off | Not used |
190→| Top-level `-z` | No timeout flag | — | Current one-pass |

Spec story 21 (“stuck pass cannot run forever”) is **not** the Hermes idle timeout. A busy agent ignores `HERMES_CRON_TIMEOUT`. A wall-clock cap needs `--run-budget` on `chat`, or a Hermes config we do not set today.

---

## Gateway, sleep, pause

Cron fires only if the **gateway ticker** is alive. A CLI chat does not tick cron. Tick is every 60s.

1→---
name: authoring-skills
description: Author a new agent skill or improve an existing one - write the SKILL.md frontmatter and description, structure the body, and fix skills that under- or over-trigger. Use when asked to create/write a skill, make a SKILL.md, improve/refactor a skill, or fix a skill's description.
version: 0.2.0
license: MIT
category: Meta / Authoring
compatibility: opencode
metadata:
  audience: skill-authors
10→  workflow: local
---

# Authoring Skills

A workflow for writing a new skill or improving an existing one so it triggers
reliably, stays maintainable, and earns its place in context. Grounded in
Anthropic's "Lessons from building Claude Code: how we use skills" (Jun 2026)
and the conventions of well-written skills in this repository.

20→A skill is a **folder, not just a markdown file**: a `SKILL.md` plus optional
`references/` (load-on-demand markdown), `scripts/` (helpers), and `assets/`
(templates). Treat the whole folder as context engineering.

## When to use

- Turning a repeatable workflow, tool/API reference, verification procedure, or
  review checklist into a reusable skill.
- An existing skill under-triggers (never fires when it should) or over-triggers
  (fires for the wrong tasks) — usually a `description` problem.
30→- A `SKILL.md` has grown unwieldy and needs splitting into `references/`.

## When NOT to use

- The behaviour is a one-off — that belongs in a note, not a skill.
- The content just restates what the model already does well (see Anti-patterns).

## Step 0 — Is a skill the right vessel?

1. **Does it fit cleanly in one category?** The best skills fit one job; ones
40→   that straddle several confuse the agent. If your idea spans two, split it.
   See [references/skill-types.md](references/skill-types.md) for the nine-category
   taxonomy and a "which bucket?" decision aid.
2. **Does it push the model off its defaults?** If not, write nothing.
3. **Will it be reused?** One-off → note. Reused → skill.

## Step 1 — Write the description first (the discovery trigger)

The agent scans every skill's `description` to decide "is there a skill for this
request?" It is **not a summary — it is a description of *when to trigger*.**
50→Write it for the model: lead with the literal phrases a user would type,
enumerate the situations it covers, add a boundary clause if a sibling skill
could also match, keep it third-person present.

Litmus test: read *only* the description and predict which prompts fire it. If
you can't, neither can the agent — iterate before touching the body. Patterns,
worked before/after examples, and the full test are in
[references/descriptions.md](references/descriptions.md).

## Step 2 — Choose the body shape
60→
Pick the smallest archetype that fits; grow it later (most good skills start as
a few lines and one gotcha):

| Archetype | Use for | Representative example |
|---|---|---|
| **Inline technique** (<80 lines, no subfolders) | A single self-contained procedure | `write-large-file` |
| **Phase / reference-table workflow** | A multi-step process where each step has depth | `gitlab-babysit-mr` |
| **Deep reference + guardrails** | A tool/API with many footguns, budgets, caveats | `glab` |

70→Don't pre-build a `references/` tree you don't yet need.

## Step 3 — Write the body

1. Open with one or two sentences on what the skill does and what it assumes.
2. **Lead with the gotchas** — the highest-signal content is what the agent gets
   wrong by default. Prefer concrete "X is actually Y" facts over generic advice;
   grow this section as new edge cases surface.
3. **Don't railroad.** Give facts and constraints, not a rigid transcript, unless
   order genuinely matters (destructive/safety steps).
80→4. **Store scripts; let the agent compose.** Ship helpers for boilerplate so the
   agent spends turns deciding what to do, not rebuilding scaffolding. Reference
   them by path relative to the skill root and say so.
5. End with an **Agent Guidelines / Rules** list if the skill has many discrete
   do/don't facts — a scannable contract the agent can re-check.

## Step 4 — Progressive disclosure: inline vs bundled

Keep `SKILL.md` to the trigger plus always-needed essentials (this repo enforces
a 150-line hard ceiling, <100 target). Push depth into files loaded on demand:
90→
- **`references/<topic>.md`** when a section serves only a sub-case, or the body
  is creeping past the length budget. Link it inline so the agent knows it exists.
- **`scripts/`** for any deterministic step. **`assets/`** for output templates.

Rule of thumb: if a heading would only matter to a fraction of invocations, it
belongs in `references/`; if every time, keep it inline.

## Step 5 — Frontmatter

100→Required: `name` (kebab-case, equal to the directory name), `description`,
`version` (semver, bumped on every change), `license`. Common optional fields:
`compatibility`, `metadata.*`. Full field reference, allowed values, and a
linting checklist: [references/frontmatter.md](references/frontmatter.md).

To start from a skeleton, copy [assets/SKILL.template.md](assets/SKILL.template.md)
— it has frontmatter stubs and commented section placeholders for each archetype.

## Step 6 — Verify before shipping

110→1. **Trigger test:** write 3–5 prompts that should fire the skill and 2–3 that
   should not; read only the `description` and predict; adjust until correct.
2. **Cold-read test:** would an agent with no prior context follow the body
   without guessing at paths or commands? Resolve every relative path.

The `opencode-refine` skill drives both tests with `opencode run`.

## Improving an existing skill

Diagnose the symptom, then make the smallest fix:
120→
- **Under-triggers** → description missing trigger phrases; add the literal words.
- **Over-triggers** → description too broad / overlaps a sibling; add a boundary.
- **Fires but underperforms** → missing gotcha, or railroading; add the failure
  to the gotchas section, loosen over-specific steps.
- **Too long / slow to load** → move sub-case sections into `references/`.

Always capture the failure as a gotcha so it can't recur — this is how skills
compound in value.

130→## Anti-patterns

- **Stating the obvious** — restating model defaults adds context cost, zero value.
- **Straddling categories** — one skill, one job.
- **Description-as-summary** — omits trigger words; the skill silently never fires.
- **Railroading** — a rigid transcript that breaks when reality differs.
- **Premature `references/`** — splitting before the skill is big enough.
- **Reconstructing boilerplate in prose** instead of shipping a script.
- **Baking in environment specifics** (paths, IDs) instead of config + ask-once.

# Authoring Skills

A workflow for writing a new skill or improving an existing one so it triggers
reliably, stays maintainable, and earns its place in context. Grounded in
Anthropic's "Lessons from building Claude Code: how we use skills" (Jun 2026)
and the conventions of well-written skills in this repository.

20→A skill is a **folder, not just a markdown file**: a `SKILL.md` plus optional
`references/` (load-on-demand markdown), `scripts/` (helpers), and `assets/`
(templates). Treat the whole folder as context engineering.

## When to use

- Turning a repeatable workflow, tool/API reference, verification procedure, or
  review checklist into a reusable skill.
- An existing skill under-triggers (never fires when it should) or over-triggers
  (fires for the wrong tasks) — usually a `description` problem.
30→- A `SKILL.md` has grown unwieldy and needs splitting into `references/`.

## When NOT to use

- The behaviour is a one-off — that belongs in a note, not a skill.
- The content just restates what the model already does well (see Anti-patterns).

## Step 0 — Is a skill the right vessel?

1. **Does it fit cleanly in one category?** The best skills fit one job; ones
40→   that straddle several confuse the agent. If your idea spans two, split it.
   See [references/skill-types.md](references/skill-types.md) for the nine-category
   taxonomy and a "which bucket?" decision aid.
2. **Does it push the model off its defaults?** If not, write nothing.
3. **Will it be reused?** One-off → note. Reused → skill.

## Step 1 — Write the description first (the discovery trigger)

The agent scans every skill's `description` to decide "is there a skill for this
request?" It is **not a summary — it is a description of *when to trigger*.**
50→Write it for the model: lead with the literal phrases a user would type,
enumerate the situations it covers, add a boundary clause if a sibling skill
could also match, keep it third-person present.

Litmus test: read *only* the description and predict which prompts fire it. If
you can't, neither can the agent — iterate before touching the body. Patterns,
worked before/after examples, and the full test are in
[references/descriptions.md](references/descriptions.md).

## Step 2 — Choose the body shape
60→
Pick the smallest archetype that fits; grow it later (most good skills start as
a few lines and one gotcha):

| Archetype | Use for | Representative example |
|---|---|---|
| **Inline technique** (<80 lines, no subfolders) | A single self-contained procedure | `write-large-file` |
| **Phase / reference-table workflow** | A multi-step process where each step has depth | `gitlab-babysit-mr` |
| **Deep reference + guardrails** | A tool/API with many footguns, budgets, caveats | `glab` |

70→Don't pre-build a `references/` tree you don't yet need.

## Step 3 — Write the body

1. Open with one or two sentences on what the skill does and what it assumes.
2. **Lead with the gotchas** — the highest-signal content is what the agent gets
   wrong by default. Prefer concrete "X is actually Y" facts over generic advice;
   grow this section as new edge cases surface.
3. **Don't railroad.** Give facts and constraints, not a rigid transcript, unless
   order genuinely matters (destructive/safety steps).
80→4. **Store scripts; let the agent compose.** Ship helpers for boilerplate so the

   do/don't facts — a scannable contract the agent can re-check.

a 150-line hard ceiling, <100 target). Push depth into files loaded on demand:
90→

belongs in `references/`; if every time, keep it inline.

— it has frontmatter stubs and commented section placeholders for each archetype.

110→1. **Trigger test:** write 3–5 prompts that should fire the skill and 2–3 that
   should not; read only the `description` and predict; adjust until correct.
2. **Cold-read test:** would an agent with no prior context follow the body
   without guessing at paths or commands? Resolve every relative path.

The `opencode-refine` skill drives both tests with `opencode run`.

Diagnose the symptom, then make the smallest fix:
120→
- **Under-triggers** → description missing trigger phrases; add the literal words.
- **Over-triggers** → description too broad / overlaps a sibling; add a boundary.

130→## Anti-patterns

- **Premature `references/`** — splitting before the skill is big enough.
- **Reconstructing boilerplate in prose** instead of shipping a script.
- **Baking in environment specifics** (paths, IDs) instead of config + ask-once.

Q1 is **B**. A helper file is not a routine object. It rides inside the Skill.

**How it looks**

This repo already uses that shape:

```
slack-pr-approve/          ← the Skill (source)
  SKILL.md                 ← names the file and the MCP steps
  scripts/
    filter-prs.sh          ← optional helper
```

`writeRoutine` copies the whole tree:

```
~/.dora/harness/<slug>/
  prompt.md
  routine.yml
  skills/slack-pr-approve/
    SKILL.md
    scripts/filter-prs.sh
```

`SKILL.md` points at the file. Example:

```
1. Poll Slack with the Scalekit tools.
   Done-when: new items are listed, or the list is empty.
2. Run scripts/filter-prs.sh on that list.
   Done-when: the script printed the keep set.
3. Approve each kept PR with the Scalekit tools.
   Done-when: each item is approved or skipped with a reason.
```

Hermes loads the Skill with `--skill`. The night pass still uses an LLM for MCP calls. The script only does local work (filter, parse, format). It cannot use Hermes MCP tokens.

1→# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
10→- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

Infer the repo from `git remote -v` — `gh` does this automatically when run inside a clone.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

20→When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either — resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

30→Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

40→- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies** — the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only — the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me` — the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

1→---
name: to-spec
description: Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the project issue tracker — no interview, just synthesis of what you've already discussed.
disable-model-invocation: true
---

This skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec. Do NOT interview the user — just synthesize what you already know.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.
10→
## Process

1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven't already. Use the project's domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you're touching.

2. Sketch out the seams at which you're going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.

The solution to the problem, from the user's perspective.

</user-story-example>

- Technical clarifications from the developer

- Schema changes

- Specific interactions

1→# ask-dora skill family

Date: 2026-08-31
Status: ready-for-agent
Source: grill in this repo, 2026-08-31. Glossary: `CONTEXT.md` (ask-dora section).
Issue: [#84](https://github.com/saif-shines/doraval/issues/84)
Tickets: #85 → then #86 and #87 in parallel → #88 → #89
Related: [Local use-case runner](../local-use-cases/spec.md) and issues #79–#83. This spec does not redo the harness CLI.

10→## Problem Statement

An internal Scalekit teammate opens a coding agent and wants help with Dora.

Today the shipped skill talks only to the Runner. It says: run `dora review --quick`, then fix, until exit 0. That is one job.

The teammate’s real start is a sentence: they type a command and describe an agent they want to run on this machine. Or they ask a normal Dora question (review, fix, unused). There is no one skill that routes both.

The harness already has a grill skill (`grill-routine`) and a routine folder. That grill is not the front door. It does not ask “is this loop-able?” first. It does not check Scalekit connectors. It does not copy skills into the routine. It is not written as a small family.

20→Matt-style idea-to-ship maps do not fit. This product is not “any software idea → ship code.” It is a **routine idea** → a **local** agent that can **loop**.

## Solution

Ship four skills under one add: `npx skills add saif-shines/doraval`.

1. **`ask-dora`** — the only name the human must remember. User-typed router. They type `/ask-dora` plus any Dora question or a routine idea.
2. **`review-with-dora`** — the old Runner loop (review → fix → exit 0). Replaces the skill named `doraval`.
3. **`grilling-for-routine`** — interview for a routine idea. Replaces `grill-routine`.
4. **`writing-for-routine`** — how to write the unattended night prompt. Original text. Same craft as a good agent document (steps, done-when, no second-person). Do not cite or copy another pack.
30→
`discover-connectors` already exists in Scalekit. Point at it. Do not author a second skill with that name.

**Route**

- A Dora job (review, fix, unused, scan) → `review-with-dora` or the matching `dora` verb.
- A **routine idea** (loop, recurring, or an agent that should keep running locally) → the routine flow.

**Routine flow**

40→1. Is it **loop-able**? Can the same prompt run on an interval? If no: say why. Stop. Do not write a routine. Route if it is a normal Dora job.
2. `grilling-for-routine`.
3. Practicality check: live Scalekit connector catalog via `discover-connectors`. Say what exists. Say what an interval job cannot do.
4. `writing-for-routine` writes the night prompt.
5. **Routine copy**: duplicate skill folders into the routine. Source is a name on this machine, a local path, or a GitHub URL. Never edit the original.
6. One live run (print the command, or run it). Missing Hermes: print official install steps. Do not fake a pass.
7. If that run works → **loop** on Hermes. Default interval 1 hour. Dora stays off OAuth. Token fail → `hermes mcp login`.

`dora harness new` starts `ask-dora`, which loads `grilling-for-routine` when the ask is a routine idea.

50→## User Stories

FileContent.content:
1→## What it does

`to-spec` turns the conversation you have just had into a **[spec](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/spec)**, and publishes it to your issue tracker as a single issue.

It does not interview you. By the time you reach for it the deciding is already done, so it synthesises what is known — from the thread, from the codebase, from your `CONTEXT.md` and ADRs — rather than opening a fresh round of questions. The spec is a record of decisions already made, not a place where new ones get made.

## When to reach for it

You invoke this by typing `/to-spec` — the [agent](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/agent) won't reach for it on its own.
10→
Reach for it when the build is too big for one agent [session](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/session) and has to survive being split across several. That is the whole trigger:

| Where you are | What to run |
| --- | --- |
| You haven't decided anything yet | [grill-with-docs](https://aihero.dev/skills-grill-with-docs) first |
| Decided, and the work fits one [context window](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/context-window) | [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement) — skip the spec |
| Decided, and the work spans several sessions | `/to-spec`, then [to-tickets](https://aihero.dev/skills-to-tickets) |
| A [wayfinder](https://aihero.dev/skills-wayfinder) map has cleared | `/to-spec #<map_issue>` |

20→## Prerequisites

`to-spec` publishes the spec as an issue, so [setup-matt-pocock-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-setup-matt-pocock-skills) must have configured a tracker and the triage-label vocabulary for this repo first. Either kind works: a real tracker like GitHub, or local markdown files under `.scratch/`, which is supported out of the box.

## The spec is a decision record

The spec exists because context windows end. Everything you settled while [grilling](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/grilling) — the shape of the solution, the choices you argued through, what you deliberately refused — is in one conversation that is about to be cleared. The spec is what survives that.

So it does not validate anything, and it does not decide anything. It captures what was decided, in your project's own vocabulary, so that a fresh session can pick the work up without you re-explaining it. Anything the spec asserts that you never actually said is a defect.

30→## Seams before prose

Before it writes a word, `to-spec` sketches the **seams** the feature will be tested at, and checks them with you. It prefers seams that already exist to new ones, and takes the highest seam it can — the ideal number across a change is one.

Those agreed seams then travel. [tdd](https://aihero.dev/skills-tdd) works only at pre-agreed seams, and [code-review](https://aihero.dev/skills-code-review) reviews the diff against the spec, so a seam nobody agreed to shows up as a review finding. The binding is indirect — it runs through this document — which is exactly why the seam conversation is worth taking seriously here rather than deferring it to implementation.

## Common questions

**Where did `/to-prd` go?**
It is this skill, renamed in v1.1. "Spec" is now the single through-line term, and the old `to-prd` slug is dead — reinstall under the new name. The pair that replaced the old vocabulary is *spec* and *tickets*: the spec is the destination and the decisions that fix it, the [tickets](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/ticket) are the execution steps that get there. If you pivot, delete the unfinished tickets and keep the spec.
40→
**Why does the spec get the `ready-for-agent` label? I don't want an agent implementing off it.**
The label means "no further triage needed" — the document is complete enough for an agent to work from. It is an input designation, not a work order. But if you run [AFK](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/afk) agents that poll for `ready-for-agent`, that distinction isn't visible to them, and they will happily try to build the whole spec in one run instead of picking up the ticket slices. This is the most-reported rough edge on the skill. Until it changes, exclude the parent spec explicitly in your AFK agent's prompt, or strip the label once `/to-tickets` has run.

**Why not go straight from grilling to `/to-tickets` and skip the spec?**
Often you should — the spec earns its step only on multi-session work. Where it pays is that the tickets are disposable and the spec isn't: each ticket is sized for one fresh context window and gets deleted or closed, while the spec stays as the one place the reasoning behind them lives. On a single-session change that buys you nothing, and you have paid an extra synthesis step where the [model](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/model) can drift. Go grilling → `/implement`.

**I just finished a wayfinder map. What do I feed it?**
The main map issue — `/to-spec #<map_issue>`, not the individual decision tickets. [wayfinder](https://aihero.dev/skills-wayfinder) produces decisions rather than deliverables, scattered across a map; `to-spec` is the step that collapses them into one buildable document. Looping the map straight into `/implement` throws that collapse away.

50→**Is the spec for me to review, or is it just for the agent?**
Mostly for the agent, and it reads that way — complete, dense, reference-heavy. The parts worth your eyes are the seams and the out-of-scope section, because those are the two places a wrong decision is cheapest to catch and most expensive to discover later. Reading the whole thing end to end is a real complaint people have, and there is no summary mode: the honest answer is that if the spec surprises you, the grilling was too shallow, not the spec too long.

**Do I keep the spec frozen once tickets start, or let the agent rewrite it?**
Nothing keeps it in sync, so in practice it is a snapshot of what you knew at that moment, and it goes stale the first time implementation teaches you something. Treat it as throwaway once the work ships. The artifacts meant to outlive it are your `CONTEXT.md` and your ADRs — if something learned during implementation deserves to last, it belongs there, not in an edited spec.

**My work is a refactor or a module boundary, not a feature. Does the template fit?**
Less well, and this is a known limitation. The template leans hard on user stories, which is the wrong shape for architectural work — you end up writing stories nobody asked for around decisions that are really about interfaces and invariants. Lean on the implementation-decisions and testing-decisions sections instead, and let the durable architectural calls land as ADRs via [grill-with-docs](https://aihero.dev/skills-grill-with-docs) rather than trying to make the spec carry them.

**Will it check the tracker for related work, or cite the ADRs it's respecting?**
60→No to both. It reads and respects the ADRs covering the area it touches, but it doesn't link them, and it doesn't search the tracker for overlapping issues before drafting — so a spec can quietly duplicate work someone already filed. Search the tracker yourself first if the area is busy.

**`/to-tickets` couldn't read my spec — it kept truncating.**
Very large specs can outgrow what a tracker issue will serve back cleanly, and there is no local copy to fall back on. The fix is context hygiene: don't [clear](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/clearing) or [compact](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/compaction) between `/to-spec` and `/to-tickets`. Run them in the same window and the spec never has to be re-fetched at all.

## It's working if

- It starts writing rather than asking you a fresh round of questions.
- It puts the seams to you before it writes, and proposes as few as it can get away with.
- It comes back in your project's nouns, not generic product-management boilerplate.
70→- Every decision in it is one you can remember making. Nothing was invented to fill a section.
- The out-of-scope section has real things in it — the things you refused are usually the most useful lines on the page.

## Where it fits

`to-spec` is a step in the main build chain, and only on the multi-session branch of it:

```txt
grill-with-docs → to-spec → to-tickets → implement → code-review
```

The spec is a record of decisions already made, not a place where new ones get made.

## When to reach for it

You invoke this by typing `/to-spec` — the [agent](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/agent) won't reach for it on its own.
10→
Reach for it when the build is too big for one agent [session](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/session) and has to survive being split across several. That is the whole trigger:

| Where you are | What to run |
| --- | --- |
| You haven't decided anything yet | [grill-with-docs](https://aihero.dev/skills-grill-with-docs) first |
| Decided, and the work fits one [context window](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/context-window) | [implement](https://aihero.dev/skills-implement) — skip the spec |
| Decided, and the work spans several sessions | `/to-spec`, then [to-tickets](https://aihero.dev/skills-to-tickets) |
| A [wayfinder](https://aihero.dev/skills-wayfinder) map has cleared | `/to-spec #<map_issue>` |

20→## Prerequisites

`to-spec` publishes the spec as an issue, so [setup-matt-pocock-skills](https://aihero.dev/skills-setup-matt-pocock-skills) must have configured a tracker and the triage-label vocabulary for this repo first. Either kind works: a real tracker like GitHub, or local markdown files under `.scratch/`, which is supported out of the box.

## The spec is a decision record

The spec exists because context windows end. Everything you settled while [grilling](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/grilling) — the shape of the solution, the choices you argued through, what you deliberately refused — is in one conversation that is about to be cleared. The spec is what survives that.

So it does not validate anything, and it does not decide anything. It captures what was decided, in your project's own vocabulary, so that a fresh session can pick the work up without you re-explaining it. Anything the spec asserts that you never actually said is a defect.

30→## Seams before prose

Before it writes a word, `to-spec` sketches the **seams** the feature will be tested at, and checks them with you. It prefers seams that already exist to new ones, and takes the highest seam it can — the ideal number across a change is one.

Those agreed seams then travel. The binding is indirect — it runs through this document — which is exactly why the seam conversation is worth taking seriously here rather than deferring it to implementation.

## Common questions

**Where did `/to-prd` go?**
It is this skill, renamed in v1.1. "Spec" is now the single through-line term, and the old `to-prd` slug is dead — reinstall under the new name. The pair that replaced the old vocabulary is *spec* and *tickets*: the spec is the destination and the decisions that fix it, the [tickets](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/ticket) are the execution steps that get there. If you pivot, delete the unfinished tickets and keep the spec.
40→
**Why does the spec get the `ready-for-agent` label? I don't want an agent implementing off it.**
The label means "no further triage needed" — the document is complete enough for an agent to work from. It is an input designation, not a work order. **Why not go straight from grilling to `/to-tickets` and skip the spec?**
Often you should — the spec earns its step only on multi-session work. Where it pays is that the tickets are disposable and the spec isn't: each ticket is sized for one fresh context window and gets deleted or closed, while the spec stays as the one place the reasoning behind them lives. On a single-session change that buys you nothing, and you have paid an extra synthesis step where the [model](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/model) can drift. Go grilling → `/implement`.

**I just finished a wayfinder map. What do I feed it?**
The main map issue — `/to-spec #<map_issue>`, not the individual decision tickets. [wayfinder](https://aihero.dev/skills-wayfinder) produces decisions rather than deliverables, scattered across a map; `to-spec` is the step that collapses them into one buildable document. Looping the map straight into `/implement` throws that collapse away.

Mostly for the agent, and it reads that way — complete, dense, reference-heavy. The parts worth your eyes are the seams and the out-of-scope section, because those are the two places a wrong decision is cheapest to catch and most expensive to discover later. Reading the whole thing end to end is a real complaint people have, and there is no summary mode: the honest answer is that if the spec surprises you, the grilling was too shallow, not the spec too long.

**Do I keep the spec frozen once tickets start, or let the agent rewrite it?**
Nothing keeps it in sync, so in practice it is a snapshot of what you knew at that moment, and it goes stale the first time implementation teaches you something. Treat it as throwaway once the work ships. The artifacts meant to outlive it are your `CONTEXT.md` and your ADRs — if something learned during implementation deserves to last, it belongs there, not in an edited spec.

**My work is a refactor or a module boundary, not a feature. Does the template fit?**
Less well, and this is a known limitation. The template leans hard on user stories, which is the wrong shape for architectural work — you end up writing stories nobody asked for around decisions that are really about interfaces and invariants. Lean on the implementation-decisions and testing-decisions sections instead, and let the durable architectural calls land as ADRs via [grill-with-docs](https://aihero.dev/skills-grill-with-docs) rather than trying to make the spec carry them.

**Will it check the tracker for related work, or cite the ADRs it's respecting?**
60→No to both. It reads and respects the ADRs covering the area it touches, but it doesn't link them, and it doesn't search the tracker for overlapping issues before drafting — so a spec can quietly duplicate work someone already filed. Search the tracker yourself first if the area is busy.

**`/to-tickets` couldn't read my spec — it kept truncating.**
Very large specs can outgrow what a tracker issue will serve back cleanly, and there is no local copy to fall back on. The fix is context hygiene: don't [clear](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/clearing) or [compact](https://www.aihero.dev/ai-coding-dictionary/compaction) between `/to-spec` and `/to-tickets`. Run them in the same window and the spec never has to be re-fetched at all.

## It's working if

- It starts writing rather than asking you a fresh round of questions.
- It puts the seams to you before it writes, and proposes as few as it can get away with.
- It comes back in your project's nouns, not generic product-management boilerplate.
70→- Every decision in it is one you can remember making. Nothing was invented to fill a section.
- The out-of-scope section has real things in it — the things you refused are usually the most useful lines on the page.

## Where it fits

`to-spec` is a step in the main build chain, and only on the multi-session branch of it:

```txt
grill-with-docs → to-spec → to-tickets → implement → code-review
```
